extracted.intended_audience: covered entities (health care providers, health insurers, group health plans, third-party administrators), legal counsel, compliance officers, and rulemaking commenters
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal guidance governing compliance with Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act (nondiscrimination in health programs and activities), including who is a covered entity, applicable nondiscrimination duties (language access, disability access, sex discrimination), and interactions with other statutory regimes (ERISA, Title IX, ADA, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on health-factor-based discrimination in group plans and insurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Group health plans and health insurance issuers offering group or individual health insurance coverage are generally prohibited from establishing any rule for eligibility, benefits, or premiums or contributions that discriminates based on any health factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory/regulatory citations provided: 26 U.S.C. 9802; 29 U.S.C. 1182; 42 U.S.C. 300gg-4; 26 CFR 54.9802-1; 29 CFR 2590.702; 45 CFR 146.121, 147.110. Use these authorities to evaluate plan terms and insurer practices for discriminatory rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party administrator (TPA) liability under Section 1557
rubrics_metrics.description: A third party administrator could be liable under section 1557 for damages arising from discriminatory terms in a self-funded employer-provided health plan if the third party administrator provided the employer with a discriminatory plan document, notwithstanding the fact that the employer subsequently adopted the plan and maintained control over its terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited case law (C.P. v. Blue Cross Blue Shield of Ill., No. 20-cv-6145, 2022 WL 17788148) supports that TPAs acting as health insurance issuers or otherwise conducting health-care-related operations may be covered entities; ERISA's plan-document decision-making requirement is no defense because ERISA does not invalidate or impair federal laws like Section 1557.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entities 'principally engaged in the business of health care' have coverage across operations
rubrics_metrics.description: If an entity is principally engaged in the business of health care, all of its operations are covered by section 1557 (e.g., finding CVS Pharmacy, Inc. to be principally engaged in health care so its PBM operations were covered).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precedent (Doe One v. CVS Pharmacy, Inc.) to assess whether nontraditional health actors (pharmacies, PBMs) are covered; coverage may extend to subsidiaries/operations like PBMs and care management arms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 1557 obligations are not necessarily displaced by ERISA plan-document duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have held that ERISA's requirement to administer a plan's terms as written is subservient to Section 1557's nondiscrimination mandate; ERISA should not be construed to impair Section 1557.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite cases such as C.P. by & through Pritchard v. Blue Cross Blue Shield of Ill. and Tovar v. Essentia Health. When plan terms conflict with nondiscrimination law, Section 1557 requirements may prevail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute of limitations for Section 1557 claims — potentially federal catchall
rubrics_metrics.description: At least one court (Tomei v. Parkwest Med. Ctr.) held that the catchall federal statute of limitations at 28 U.S.C. 1658(a) applies to claims under Section 1557 because Section 1557 lacks an express statute of limitations; other courts have applied Rehabilitation Act limitations in some cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should consult controlling case law because courts differ (see Solis v. Our Lady of the Lake Ascension Cmty. Hosp., Inc. for a contrasting application).

rubrics_metrics.name: Language access and LEP obligations (translated materials, taglines, language assistance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Covered entities should provide translated Notice of Nondiscrimination, Statement of Nondiscrimination, and taglines required by the 2016 Rule and offer language assistance to persons with limited English proficiency (LEP).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References: OCR Translated Resources for Covered Entities; CEFR; AHRQ guide Improving Patient Safety Systems for Patients With LEP; HHS Language Access Annual Progress Report. Use these resources to determine appropriate languages, translated content, and methods of providing language assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreter relationship and HIPAA obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining the relationship between the interpreter and the covered entity is a covered entity's HIPAA obligation and is unchanged by Section 1557 or this part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covered entities should review OCR's HIPAA FAQs regarding whether an interpreter is a business associate and other HIPAA-related obligations when engaging interpreters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for video remote interpreting (VRI) in medical settings
rubrics_metrics.description: VRI standards (e.g., size of the video image to ensure the screen shows one's face, arms, hands, and fingers) are governed by certain ADA/ADA-regulatory provisions (28 CFR 35.160(d)(2)), but §92.201(f)(2) in this final rule does not regulate the size of the video image because that component is less relevant for oral interpretation between English and non-English languages or two non-English spoken languages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to NAD's Minimum Standards for Video Remote Interpreting Services in Medical Settings and settlement agreements/case law cited for operational expectations in VRI. Consider differing regulatory emphases when implementing VRI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective communication and program accessibility for people with disabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The central inquiry under the ADA and Section 504 is whether the program, when viewed in its entirety, is readily accessible to and usable by individuals with disabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Bird v. Lewis & Clark Coll. and related ADA/Section 504 regulations (28 CFR 35.150(a); 45 CFR 84.22(a)). Use OCR resources on Disability Resources for Effective Communication and Section 508/VPAT guidance for ICT accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 508 information and communication technology (ICT) accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 508 of the Rehabilitation Act imposes accessibility requirements for information and communication technology that Federal departments and agencies develop, procure, maintain, or use; use the Voluntary Product Accessibility Template (VPAT) to document accessibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference Section508.gov VPAT and 36 CFR part 1194, appendix A. Agencies and covered entities should use these tools for ICT procurement and compliance evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of reasonable accommodations and support persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Covered entities must ensure reasonable access to support persons (e.g., family, aides) in health-care settings and make reasonable modifications and accommodations for individuals with disabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR resolutions and bulletins (e.g., OCR resolves complaints about reasonable access to support persons during COVID-19) demonstrate enforcement expectations. Consult settlement agreements and OCR guidance for practical implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and interpretation of 'sex discrimination' — evolving case law (Bostock, Neese)
rubrics_metrics.description: OCR acknowledges that at least one court has held that it would be a misapplication of Bostock to interpret the definition of 'sex discrimination' under Section 1557 and Title IX to include gender identity and sexual orientation (Neese v. Becerra); the Department appealed that decision and is not applying the challenged interpretation to members of the Neese class pending appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because courts differ, covered entities and litigants should monitor appellate outcomes; OCR's interpretive positions may be subject to litigation and limited application depending on court rulings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multidisciplinary evidence and research to inform nondiscrimination policies
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department cites a broad body of social science, medical, legal, and administrative evidence (studies on LEP, disability, LGBTQ health disparities, structural racism, transplant access, etc.) to justify regulatory choices and to inform expectations for covered entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory compliance and policy design should consider empirical findings cited (e.g., studies on LEP impacts, CLAS standards, research on discrimination's health effects) when developing language-access plans, anti-discrimination policies, and equity-focused interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction with other civil-rights enforcement regimes and agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1557 implementation and enforcement intersects with other civil-rights laws and agencies (EEOC for employment discrimination, DOJ Title IX guidance, state/federal statutes cited), and related regulations (e.g., title IX, section 504, Age Act) provide complementary standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covered entities should coordinate compliance across overlapping regimes and consult agency resources (EEOC overview, DOJ Title IX Legal Manual, cross-referenced CFR provisions) for multi-law obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translated and accessible consumer-facing materials (practical resources)
rubrics_metrics.description: OCR provides translated resources for covered entities (translated Notice of Nondiscrimination, Statement of Nondiscrimination, and taglines) and links to practical guidance to promote equitable access to language services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use OCR-provided templates and HHS/OMH grant programs and published resources (e.g., CLAS standards, AHRQ LEP guides) when preparing consumer notices, taglines, and translated materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional clinical standards relevant to nondiscrimination (informed consent, ethical care)
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional standards such as the AMA's guidance on informed consent are referenced as relevant to nondiscrimination and provision of ethically appropriate, non-discriminatory care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clinical policies should align nondiscrimination duties with professional ethical norms (e.g., informed consent practices) and relevant guidance cited in the rulemaking.
